analysis.one_liner: Directs EPA to ban all manufacture, import, use, and sale of asbestos within two years.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote; it died in the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee after being referred on the day it was introduced.
analysis.plain_summary: Asbestos causes cancer, but the United States still allowed it to be imported and used in some products. This bill would have forced the Environmental Protection Agency to identify every current use of asbestos and, within 18 months, write rules that permanently eliminate human exposure to it. The President could waive the ban for a narrow national-security use with no alternative. The bill was referred to the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee and never moved again before that Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary people—workers in demolition, construction, auto repair, and manufacturing, their families, and residents of older buildings—would gain from a hard deadline to end exposure to a known carcinogen. The bill names deadlines the agency must meet rather than leaving the pace to regulators.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Workers and residents exposed to asbestos

how_it_helps.text: Requires EPA, within 90 days, to identify and publish an assessment of all current imports, sales, uses of, and exposures to asbestos [S2][S3].

Requires EPA, within 18 months, to impose rules prohibiting the manufacture, processing, use, distribution, and disposal of asbestos and asbestos-containing products, chosen to permanently eliminate the possibility of exposure [S2][S3].
Sets firm deadlines in the law itself, so the ban cannot be delayed indefinitely by an agency that chooses to move slowly [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Companies that still import, process, or use asbestos—including the chlor-alkali industry, which used asbestos in chlorine production, and makers of asbestos-containing products—would bear the cost of switching to alternatives. Some compliance costs could pass through to consumers.

drawbacks.text: The ban is nearly absolute: it instructs EPA to pick requirements that 'permanently eliminate the possibility of exposure,' without weighing costs, which is a stricter standard than typical environmental rules and could be challenged as unworkable for trace amounts in legacy products [S3].
Industries with no off-the-shelf substitute would face disruption; the only escape valve is a presidential national-security exemption limited to three years per determination [S2][S3].
A fast timetable puts heavy demands on EPA's assessment and rule-writing capacity within 18 months [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The health case is strong: asbestos is a known carcinogen, and ending exposure protects workers and the public. The main honest costs fall on a small set of industrial users who would need substitutes, and the bill's zero-exposure standard is unusually strict. The trade-off favors the ban, but the bill still would have required careful implementation rules to work in practice.

outcome.mechanism: It was read once and referred to the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee on the day it was introduced, and the committee never took it up before that Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Jeff Merkley and seven Senate colleagues introduced the bill on November 2, 2017 [S3][S5].
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Environment and Public Works the same day [S5].
No further action—no hearing, no markup, no floor vote—appears in the action history before the 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019 [S5].
All 11 cosponsors were Democrats or the chamber's Independent, and no Republican signed on [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Companies that still profit from importing and using asbestos—along with any other opponents of a ban—were better off, because the bill died in committee without ever facing a vote.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Asbestos importers and opponents of a ban

industries.industry: Asbestos importers and processors (including chlor-alkali producers)
industries.note: The bill would have banned the import, manufacture, and use of asbestos within about two years, ending a legal pathway that still existed in the U.S. These companies profit from a substance that causes cancer in exposed workers and the public.
Products containing asbestos could no longer be made, sold, or distributed in commerce, forcing a switch to alternatives.

The bill restricts handling and disposal of asbestos-containing material, adding compliance work, while workers in these industries are among the most heavily exposed and would benefit most from the ban.
